title: Deliver a useful detection run
description: Understand recording targets, track coordinates, source identity and safe redelivery.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Imagine a fictional producer that has finished tracking objects in a recording. What does it send Hub?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: One detection run bundles tracks from one source for one recording. Identify the target using the stable recording key or the documented analysis identifier. The recording key is not the media document's database identifier.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can the producer choose an API push or a workflow result?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Yes, detection supports both through the shared ingest path. The delivery choice doesn't change the run's data shape. Keep the producer name, version and logical run identity meaningful.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Our producer uses pixel boxes. Will Hub guess the frame dimensions?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: No. Supply the required oriented media dimensions for pixel coordinates, or send valid normalized coordinates. The preferred rectangle uses its top-left corner, width and height, not centre coordinates. Tracks connect a subject's boxes across frames.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What if the producer has only one box for an object?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A single-box track is valid. Keep frame order and identifiers consistent, inspect validation warnings, and distinguish a stored run with reported rejected boxes from a completely rejected result.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: The network drops after delivery and our producer retries. How do we avoid inventing a second result?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Send the same source run identifier for the same logical run. Hub upserts by recording key and source run identity. Re-delivery replaces that run; a new identity creates a separate run. Different sources can coexist without being merged or voted together.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Does a detection automatically become a human-readable timeline marker?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: No. Geometry and timeline meaning are separate contracts. Emit a marker when you need that annotation and link its track reference correctly. These are finalized recording results, not a live-stream detection protocol.

editorialStyle.tone: A short, high-level introduction for a first-time listener. Explain why the topic matters, build one mental model, and suggest one next action. Sound like two colleagues, not a narrated manual.
editorialStyle.scope: Aim for four to five minutes and roughly 500-550 spoken words. Use one fictional example and four short chapters. Leave identifiers, form limits, configuration, migration mechanics, and troubleshooting checklists in the linked guide. Keep essential caveats as practical consequences.
editorialStyle.humour: Optional: one or two brief, relevant light moments are enough. Prefer a relatable analogy over a separate joke. Never pad the overview with banter.
editorialStyle.reactions: Use occasional short, natural responses such as 'Oh, that makes sense' or 'Wait, so...' followed by a real question. Avoid repetitive praise, canned agreement, and filler.
editorialStyle.laughter: Optional: at most one or two light reactions such as 'Ha, fair point.' Never insert [laughs], SSML, or repeated ha-ha strings. These are spoken reactions, not a guarantee of genuine laughter from the current speech engine.
editorialStyle.intonation: Write real questions with question marks, use contractions, alternate short and longer sentences, and make contrasts explicit. Let punctuation and sentence rhythm suggest curiosity, surprise, and emphasis. Avoid all-caps shouting, excessive exclamation marks, and artificial pause tags.
editorialStyle.guardrails: Keep technical claims source-backed. Never mock the listener, joke about real victims, minimize security or data-loss risks, or let humour replace an explanation. Personality is optional; accuracy and clarity are not.
